title: Ancient Computer Found in a Sunken Rusty Lump?
narration: What if a rusted lump was an ancient computer? You hear about a 2nd‑century BC Greek device that predicts eclipses decades ahead. It sits in a wooden case about 34 cm by 18 cm by 9 cm. Inside, 35 bronze gears mesh, thirty still visible. The gears model the Moon’s irregular orbit, a trick first described by Hipparchus. X‑ray scans revealed the gear train and faint inscriptions. The device could forecast Sun and Moon positions far into the future. So that rusted lump was an ancient computer.

title: How a Sunken Treasure Became a Museum Star
narration: Ever wonder how a rusted lump turned into a star exhibit? The wreck off Antikythera yielded statues, glass, coins and the mechanism, which arrived at Athens’ National Archaeological Museum. On 17 May 1902 Valerios Stais and his cousin Spyridon spotted a gear wheel inside, sparking the first study. The artifact broke into three main fragments, now divided into 82 pieces, with four fragments containing gears. The largest gear measures about 13 cm in diameter and originally had 223 teeth. That rusted lump truly became a museum star.

title: Inside the Bronze Brain of the Antikythera
narration: How did a hand‑crank move the heavens? The mechanism contains thirty‑five bronze gears, though only thirty are clearly visible in the surviving fragments. The biggest wheel is about 13 cm across with 223 teeth. Turning the original hand crank would have driven this crown gear, moving the date pointer and all other dials together. The gear train allowed the device to follow the motions of the Moon and the Sun through the zodiac, to predict eclipses and to model the Moon’s irregular orbit. So a hand‑crank moves the heavens.
